Attachment A 
Page 1 of 13 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.   
)  
Docket No. EL25-49-000 
)  
Docket No. EL25-49-001 
) 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities  
) 
Docket No. AD24-11-000 
) 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC  
)  
Docket No. EL25-20-000 
v.  
 
) 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.   
)  
(Consolidated) 
REPLY TESTIMONY 
OF 
LANCE SCHAFER 
I.
INTRODUCTION  
1 
Q.  
Please state your name, title, business address, and provide your professional 
2 
background and relevant experience. 
3 
A. 
My name is Lance Schafer, and my business address is 293 Boston Post Road West, 
4 
Marlborough, MA 01752. I am a Senior Project Manager with Concentric Energy 
5 
Advisors, Inc. My professional background and relevant experience was provided as 
6 
Exhibit No. PTO-0002 to the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners’ Initial Brief filed on 
7 
February 23, 2026 in these proceedings. 
8 
Q. 
Have you previously submitted testimony in these proceedings? 
9 
A. 
Yes. I submitted testimony on behalf of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (“PJM 
10 
Transmission Owners”)1 as part of the Direct Joint Testimony filed on February 23, 2026, 
11 
and as part of the Joint Rebuttal Testimony filed on April 24, 2026 in these proceedings. 
12 
1
For purposes of this reply testimony and the accompanying answer, the PJM Transmission Owners are:  
American Electric Power Service Corporation on behalf of its affiliates, Appalachian Power Company, Indiana

Attachment A 
Page 2 of 13 
II.
BACKGROUND 
1 
Q. 
What is the background of this proceeding? 
2 
A. 
On December 18, 2025, the Commission issued its order in PJM Interconnection. L.L.C., 
3 
193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“Order”). In the Order, the Commission found that PJM 
4 
Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) “is unjust 
5 
and unreasonable because it does not contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity 
6 
or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to generators serving 
7 
Co-Located Load and Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Co-
8 
Located Load.”2 Specifically, the Commission found PJM’s Tariff “unjust and 
9 
unreasonable because it does not include types of transmission service that reflect Eligible 
10 
Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Loads that are willing and able to limit 
11 
their use of the transmission system under certain conditions.”3
12 
The Commission ordered PJM to offer three new forms of transmission service 
13 
under its Tariff, and identified these three new forms of transmission service as: (i) Firm 
14 
Contract Demand transmission service; (ii) Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission 
15 
Michigan Power Company, Kentucky Power Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling 
Power Company, AEP Appalachian Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, 
Inc., AEP Kentucky Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Ohio Transmission Company, Inc., and AEP West Virginia 
Transmission Company, Inc.; The Dayton Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio; Dominion Energy Services, 
Inc. on behalf of Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy Business 
Services, LLC for Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc. and Duke Energy Ohio, Inc.; Duquesne Light Company; East 
Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc.; Exelon Corporation on behalf of its affiliates Atlantic City Electric Company, 
Baltimore Gas and Electric Company, Commonwealth Edison Company, Commonwealth Edison Company of 
Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & Light Company, PECO Energy Company, and Potomac Electric Power Company; 
FirstEnergy Service Company, on behalf of its affiliates American Transmission Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central 
Power & Light Company, Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, The Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela 
Power Company, Keystone Appalachian Transmission Company, and Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company 
(collectively, the “FirstEnergy Companies”); PPL Electric Utilities Corporation; Public Service Electric and Gas 
Company; Rockland Electric Company; and the Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative. 
2
Order at P 2. 
3
Id.

Attachment A 
Page 3 of 13 
service; and (iii) interim, non-firm transmission service.4 The Commission also established 
1 
a paper hearing to determine the just and reasonable rates, terms, and conditions for these 
2 
new transmission services.5
3 
III.
PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY 
4 
Q. 
What is the purpose of your testimony?  
5 
A.   
The purpose of my testimony is to support the Answer of the PJM Transmission Owners 
6 
submitted in response to the Motion for Leave and Answer of Constellation Energy 
7 
Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) filed on May 11, 2026 in these proceedings. In 
8 
particular, I respond to the Reply Testimony of Zachary Ming, filed on behalf of 
9 
Constellation on May 11, 2026. Mr. Ming’s testimony replies to the PJM Transmission 
10 
Owners’ April 24, 2026 Reply Brief, including specifically the Joint Rebuttal Testimony 
11 
that accompanied that Reply Brief concerning the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal for 
12 
calculating a Grid Reliance Charge. 
13 
IV.
REBUTTAL TO MR. MING’S REPLY TESTIMONY ON THE GRID RELIANCE 
14 
CHARGE 
15 
Q. 
What is the Grid Reliance Charge? 
16 
A. 
The PJM Transmission Owners are proposing to charge a Grid Reliance Charge to Eligible 
17 
Customers6 taking the new Contract Demand services based on the difference between the 
18 
amount of their firm contract demand for Firm Contract Demand Service and their total 
19 
(gross) on-site load. The proposed Grid Reliance Charge is designed to reflect the costs of 
20 
using the transmission system to deliver black start and regulation services, as well as 
21 
4
Id. at P 160. 
5
Id. at PP 2, 194. 
6
Capitalized terms that are not otherwise defined shall have the meanings set forth in the PJM Tariff.

Attachment A 
Page 4 of 13 
providing the inherent benefits that all customers, including Contract Demand customers, 
1 
receive as a result of their synchronization to and reliance on the grid. The Grid Reliance 
2 
Charge also recognizes the costs associated with the operations, maintenance, and other 
3 
activities that PJM transmission owners will need to perform for the grid and to 
4 
accommodate the increased number of protection schemes that will be required for Co-
5 
Located Load customers.   
6 
Q. 
How do the PJM Transmission Owners propose to calculate the Grid Reliance 
7 
Charge? 
8 
A. 
The PJM Transmission Owners propose to calculate a Grid Reliance Charge for each PJM 
9 
zone based on determining an average fixed percentage of the portion of transmission 
10 
depreciation and operations and maintenance expense associated with providing grid 
11 
reliance services, and then applying that average fixed percentage to each PJM 
12 
Transmission Owner’s Attachment H annual transmission revenue requirement.   
13 
Q. 
Mr. Ming claims that the PJM Transmission Owners “fail to address the fundamental 
14 
shortcoming of their proposal – a transmission system built only to deliver ancillary 
15 
services would be nowhere near as large or expensive as a transmission system built 
16 
to serve peak demand.”7  Do you agree? 
17 
A. 
No. Mr. Ming’s claim is incorrect. First, Mr. Ming continues to assume, erroneously, that 
18 
the sole purpose of the Grid Reliance Charge is to recover costs associated with the delivery 
19 
of ancillary services. As I have explained, the Grid Reliance Charge is not limited to 
20 
recovering the costs associated with the delivery of ancillary services, but rather is intended 
21 
to reflect the full suite of benefits that Co-Located Load will receive by virtue of the fact 
22 
7
Reply Testimony of Zachary Ming at 9:14-16 (“Ming Reply Testimony”).

Attachment A 
Page 5 of 13 
that it will be interconnected to the integrated transmission system, and not islanded. Mr. 
1 
Ming simply ignores these benefits, which as I discussed in my previous testimony include  
2 
delivering ancillary services and a suite of essential reliability services, such as frequency 
3 
support, inertia, voltage stability, fault current capability, ride-through and protection 
4 
coordination, and providing sufficient short-circuit capability.   
5 
Mr. Ming’s other conceptual critique regarding the alleged unprecedented nature 
6 
of the Transmission Owners’ proposal fares no better. The Contract Demand Transmission 
7 
Services that the Commission has directed here are themselves based on the novel premise 
8 
that load will connect to the system and take transmission service without the transmission 
9 
provider identifying and constructing upgrades to facilitate the full amount of load. Thus, 
10 
the design of the Grid Reliance Charge reflects the unique circumstances of this 
11 
proceeding, and the transmission services that the Commission has directed here.   
12 
Finally, Mr. Ming’s attempt to distinguish his proposal from the PJM Transmission 
13 
Owners’ on the basis that his is somehow more “principled” rather than what he 
14 
characterizes as an “improvised” approach by the Transmission Owners is spurious.8 As I 
15 
explained in my previous testimony, and discuss further below, Mr. Ming’s “minimum 
16 
system” methodology has no relevance here, and even if it did, his proposed application is 
17 
flawed and superficial. Thus, it is Mr. Ming who is attempting to defend what is clearly a 
18 
contrived effort by Constellation to attempt to minimize the Grid Reliance Charge in order 
19 
to reduce their own costs at the expense of other ratepayers.      
20 
21 
22 
8
Ming Reply Testimony at 10:16-21, 12:11-12, 18:1-3.

Attachment A 
Page 6 of 13 
Q. 
Does Mr. Ming offer an alternative to the PJM Transmission Owners’ method for 
1 
calculating the Grid Reliance Charge? 
2 
A. 
Yes. Although Mr. Ming supports the application of a Grid Reliance Charge, he continues 
3 
to argue that the Commission should reject the PJM Transmission Owners’ Grid Reliance 
4 
Charge and adopt a charge based on the “minimum system method.”   
5 
Q. 
Mr. Ming states that your April 24, 2026 Joint Rebuttal Testimony reflects a 
6 
misunderstanding of the minimum system method and how its results should be 
7 
used.9  How do you respond? 
8 
A. 
Mr. Ming is incorrect. Mr. Ming’s statement is in reaction to my criticism that his 
9 
recommended 6.2% minimum system percentage only includes certain plant balances and 
10 
does not include any other element typically included in a transmission revenue 
11 
requirement, such as rate of return, taxes, depreciation, and operation and maintenance 
12 
expense.10 I pointed this out in response to Mr. Ming’s argument that the PJM Transmission 
13 
Owners’ proposal was deficient because it excluded certain cost of service components, 
14 
such as rate of return and taxes.   
 
15 
Mr. Ming’s result is the ratio of his calculated minimum system plant amount to 
16 
the total plant amount for the accounts he included in his study. A plant ratio is indeed 
17 
consistent with the expected output of a distribution minimum system study. However, Mr. 
18 
Ming then takes this plant ratio, whose purpose is only to identify the minimum-system-
19 
related portions of certain plant accounts, and applies it to the entire transmission revenue 
20 
9
Ming Reply Testimony at 17:3-12. 
10
See Joint Rebuttal Testimony of Peter Blazunas, Lance Schafer, and Hanhan Hammer, Exhibit No. PTO-
0005 at 26.

Attachment A 
Page 7 of 13 
requirement. This is methodologically unsound because the results of a minimum-system 
1 
study are not intended to be applied to a revenue requirement.  
2 
Q. 
If the result of a minimum system study is not intended to be applied to a revenue 
3 
requirement, why does Mr. Ming use the result for this purpose?   
4 
A. 
Mr. Ming incorrectly believes that the purpose of a minimum system study is to produce a 
5 
result that can be applied to a revenue requirement.  He states that “[t]he minimum system 
6 
uses the ratio of replacement costs for both the minimum system and actual system to 
7 
identify what portion of the entire revenue requirement is attributable to the minimum 
8 
system. It does not omit any element of the revenue requirement.”11 However, as noted just 
9 
above, Mr. Ming’s recommended 6.2% minimum system percentage was calculated by 
10 
comparing gross plant amounts in certain plant accounts. Mr. Ming is therefore taking a 
11 
ratio that he developed from studying certain gross-plant account balances and applying 
12 
that ratio to the entire revenue requirement. But a gross-plant ratio is not directly applicable 
13 
to the entire revenue requirement.  
14 
Q. 
Does the minimum system method use either book cost or replacement cost to 
15 
determine the minimum system portion of the accounts included in the minimum 
16 
system study? 
17 
A. 
Plant balances developed either on a book-cost or replacement-cost basis are used to 
18 
compare the “minimum system” plant balances with the total plant balances for the 
19 
accounts included in the study. This is done to determine the percentage of plant in those 
20 
specific accounts associated with the minimum system. However, contrary to Mr. Ming’s 
21 
11
Ming Reply Testimony at 17:5-9 (emphasis added).

Attachment A 
Page 8 of 13 
assertions, the minimum system study does not develop a result that appropriately describes 
1 
the minimum-system portion of the entire revenue requirement.   
2 
Q. 
Does the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioner’s Electric Cost 
3 
Allocation Manual (“NARUC Manual”) state that the purpose of the minimum 
4 
system method is to develop a result that can be applied to a revenue requirement?
5 
A. 
No. The NARUC Manual clearly explains that the minimum system method’s  purpose is 
6 
to classify distribution plant. The NARUC Manual states the following: 
7 
Classifying distribution plant with the minimum-size method assumes that a 
8 
minimum size distribution system can be built to serve the minimum loading 
9 
requirements of the customer. The minimum-size method involves determining the 
10 
minimum size pole, conductor, cable, transformer, and service that is currently 
11 
installed by the utility. Normally, the average book cost for each piece of equipment 
12 
determines the price of all installed units. Once determined for each primary plant 
13 
account, the minimum size distribution system is classified as customer-related 
14 
costs. The demand-related costs for each account are the difference between the 
15 
total investment in the account and customer-related costs.12
16 
17 
The minimum system study, as explained above, serves to classify portions of certain 
18 
accounts as either customer (i.e., pertaining to the minimum distribution system) or demand 
19 
related. Mr. Ming’s result of 6.2% merely means that, of the plant accounts included in his 
20 
study, he determined that 6.2% of the balances are related to a hypothetical minimum 
21 
system. Therefore, Mr. Ming’s calculation does not represent true revenue requirement for 
22 
the minimum system represented by that 6.2%.   
23 
24 
25 
12
National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, Electric Cost Allocation Manual (Jan. 1992), at 
90-91.

Attachment A 
Page 9 of 13 
Q. 
In addition to the NARUC Manual, do any other commonly referenced works of cost 
1 
allocation describe the purpose of the minimum system study? 
2 
A. 
Yes. Lawrence J. Vogt’s commonly referenced book Electricity Pricing, Engineering 
3 
Principles and Methodologies also describes that the purpose of the minimum system study 
4 
is to classify certain plant as either demand or customer related.  It adds:  
5 
[O]n the principle of cost causation, some distribution facilities can be classified as 
6 
purely demand related, while other distribution facilities can be classified as purely 
7 
customer related. A substantial amount of distribution plant investment has cost 
8 
causation attributes of both demand and customer cost components. For instance, a 
9 
line transformer is both customer related and demand related as it provides both a 
10 
load and a no-load function. This distinction is derived through a minimum 
11 
distribution system analysis of poles, conductors and a variety of line equipment . . 
12 
. .”13
13 
14 
Neither Mr. Vogt’s book nor the NARUC Manual, nor any other industry manual on cost 
15 
allocation that I am aware of, supports the notion that the purpose of the minimum system 
16 
study is to produce a ratio that can be applied to a revenue requirement.  
17 
Q. 
Mr. Ming states that the minimum system uses “the ratio of replacement costs for 
18 
both the minimum system and actual system to identify what portion of the entire
19 
revenue requirement is attributable to the minimum system.”14  How does the 6.2% 
20 
represent the minimum system portion of the entire revenue requirement?
21 
A. 
It does not. In his minimum system study, Mr. Ming determined that 6.2% of the plant in 
22 
the following accounts were related to a transmission minimum system: overhead 
23 
conductors, poles, towers, and substations.15 He uses plant balances—not a revenue 
24 
requirement—to derive the 6.2%. To be clear, plant balances are exactly what an analyst 
25 
13
Lawrence H. Vogt, P.E., Electricity Pricing, Engineering Principles and Methodologies (2009), at 495. 
14
See Ming Reply Testimony at 17:5-8. 
15
See Constellation March 25, 2026 Reply Brief, Testimony of Zachary Ming at 20:1.

Attachment A 
Page 10 of 13 
should use in a minimum system study—because the object of the study is classification, 
1 
not the determination of a minimum system revenue requirement. Mr. Ming then applies 
2 
his 6.2% result to the entire transmission revenue requirement. This is a methodological 
3 
leap that is not in any way a component of a distribution minimum system study. In short, 
4 
Mr. Ming is comparing apples to oranges in an attempt to arrive at a result that has a veneer 
5 
of principled objectivity. But Mr. Ming’s flawed application of the minimum system 
6 
methodology underscores the inappropriateness of his recommendation to use the 
7 
minimum system study for purposes of establishing the Grid Reliance Charge. 
8 
Q. 
Are there any other problems with the manner in which Mr. Ming conducted his 
9 
minimum system study? 
10 
A. 
Yes. Moving beyond the misapplication of the minimum system study approach, in 
11 
conducting his minimum system study, Mr. Ming uses wood distribution poles as a 
12 
substitute for transmission poles.  
13 
Q. 
How does Mr. Ming defend his decision to use wood distribution poles as a substitute 
14 
for transmission poles? 
15 
Mr. Ming justifies his use of wood poles by stating he did so “because a minimum system 
16 
is a theoretical system designed to deliver a de minimis amount of electricity as opposed 
17 
to a system designed to serve peak demand.”16 However, Mr. Ming’s proposal to substitute 
18 
wood distribution poles for transmission poles is inappropriate and not supported in 
19 
industry literature. For example, the NARUC Manual states that “the minimum-size 
20 
method involves determining the minimum size pole, conductor, cable, transformer, and 
21 
16
Ming Reply Testimony at 15:13-15.

Attachment A 
Page 11 of 13 
service that is currently installed by the utility.”17 I am not aware of any instance where a 
1 
transmission owner has installed wood distribution poles for the purposes of providing 
2 
transmission service.  
3 
Q. 
How does Mr. Ming attempt to justify his minimum system study based on the use of 
4 
distribution equipment? 
5 
A. 
Mr. Ming claims that his “theoretical” minimum system, based on the use of distribution 
6 
equipment, is justified because it represents the “cost-causation basis for determining the 
7 
portion of the system that is necessary to provide ancillary services.”18
8 
Q. 
Do you agree with this claim? 
9 
A. 
No. On the one hand, Mr. Ming justifies the use of distribution equipment in his minimum 
10 
system calculation as being acceptable because his minimum system is only “theoretical” 
11 
(i.e., it doesn’t exist). On the other hand, he says this theoretical minimum system 
12 
composed of distribution equipment represents the very system necessary to deliver 
13 
ancillary services to real-world transmission customers. These two statements are 
14 
contradictory. Also, I am not aware of any industry manual on cost allocation that supports 
15 
Mr. Ming’s claim that the minimum system method results in a system that is the 
16 
appropriate size to supply ancillary services. 
17 
18 
19 
20 
17
National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, Electric Cost Allocation Manual (Jan. 1992), at 
90 (emphasis added). 
18
Ming Reply Testimony at 8:12-16.

Attachment A 
Page 12 of 13 
Q. 
Is Mr. Ming’s recommendation to employ the minimum system method in calculating 
1 
the Grid Reliance Charge consistent with cost causation principles? 
2 
A. 
No. Mr. Ming states that his recommendation to employ the minimum system method in 
3 
calculating the Grid Reliance Charge is based on principles of cost causation.19 This is 
4 
simply not the case because the minimum system method is only appropriate for and 
5 
applicable to distribution level service. Mr. Ming ignores the very purpose of the minimum 
6 
system study, and inappropriately and inaccurately attempts to translate the methodology 
7 
to calculate a transmission service rate. By then misinterpreting the results as being 
8 
applicable to the entire transmission revenue requirement, Mr. Ming abandons all cost-
9 
causation principles that exist in a minimum-system study approach.  
10 
Q. 
Please summarize your recommendation regarding Mr. Ming’s testimony? 
11 
A. 
Mr. Ming’s proposal to employ the minimum system method in calculating the Grid 
12 
Reliance Charge is fundamentally flawed. First, Mr. Ming did not conduct his minimum 
13 
system study correctly because he included distribution equipment not installed for 
14 
transmission service. Second, Mr. Ming applies the result of his minimum-system study to 
15 
the entire transmission revenue requirement, which is contrary to the purpose of the study. 
16 
Third, the minimum system method only is appropriate for and applicable to distribution-
17 
level service. It is entirely inappropriate to apply the minimum system method to calculate 
18 
a transmission service rate. The Commission should reject Mr. Ming’s proposal and accept 
19 
the PJM Transmission Owners’ just and reasonable mechanism for determining the Grid 
20 
Reliance Charge.    
21 
22 
19
Id.

Attachment A 
Page 13 of 13 
Q. 
Does this complete your testimony at this time? 
1 
A. 
Yes.
2
